description: We are a small, passionate team focused on trying to help farmers make better decisions using data.
summary:
Croptimizing is a web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that protect their soil and still hold up even as water supplies/prices change. The idea is to treat each farm like an investment portfolio: each acre is an investment, water is the budget, and soil health is like an ESG score. By doing so, we ultimately help farmers conserve scarce resources.

Farmers just answer simple questions, such as their estimated water budget, and then receive a comprehensive crop rotation plan that includes estimated profit, impact on soil (bare months, nitrogen-fixing acres, crop diversity, etc.), risks (accounting for heat and frost months), evidence, and more for each rotation. 

We specifically built this for Pinal County, Arizona, where farms lost all Colorado River water in 2023 and 2024. On average, the suggested plan makes an estimated $230 more per acre in an average year. Essentially, we are helping farmers create the crop rotation that minimizes risk and maximizes reward.
details:
Croptimizing is a tool that helps farmers easily create crop rotations that maximize reward while minimizing risk regarding inputs such as water.

To create the site, we pulled 7,305 days of NASA POWER daily weather data for Pinal County and ran it through the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method to get reference evapotranspiration. To calculate water usage, we took crop coefficients across each crop's season, subtracted effective rainfall, and then divided by irrigation efficiency. These values are either entered by the farmer or come from NASA POWER. We also estimate the days above 110°F and at or below freezing in each month, which is how we mark risky months. Estimated profit is calculated from USDA NASS data. NASA GRACE and GRACE-FO are used to calculate water input costs, and from this we learned that water stored underground in central Arizona has fallen about 9 cm since 2005, further necessitating our site.

We backtested the model on data it wasn't trained on (from 2005 - 2014), and the suggested plan averaged $357 per acre vs. $107 for the current plan cut back to fit. In the worst years, our plans lost $126 per acre compared to $232 per acre for the default plans' averages. These gains go beyond just increasing profit, though. On average, our suggested plan earns/saves $60 more per acre in the worst one-in-five years for water; raises the soil score from 63 to 74; and assigns nitrogen-fixing crops to 215 more acres. On average, this saves 0.9 acre-feet of water, which is about 200 million gallons for a 640-acre farm.

Croptimizing also allows the impact of water cuts to actually be visualized: you can see the real impact of a shrinking water budget on soil quality, input costs, and revenue. Because NASA POWER and GRACE cover the whole planet, this method could be applied to many more regions once their crop budgets and prices are added. GRACE already shows similar declines of water stored underground in California's Central Valley (~20 cm), and northwest India (~75 cm), so this application would definitely be useful in other regions with slight modifications.

What makes Croptimizing creative is its perspective. Treating a farm like an investment portfolio is useful when considering the goal, and portfolio theory and other financial models have been used in agricultural economics before, but these rarely actually reach farmers and are seldom used in the context of water budgets and soil-health floors. Croptimizing's site dives into the math behind these and also allows farmers to move along the efficient frontier (by providing crop rotations with higher expected revenue for higher expected risk) or analyze other relationships such as soil quality vs. profit. Furthermore, these plans can get stress-tested on a dedicated simulations page to show how these rotations would have held up against record heat or sudden water supply cutoffs.

Although our application was built around mathematical models, Croptimizing explains and visualizes these concepts simply; in fact, every aspect of this site was designed around simplicity, versatility, and utility. Croptimizing works on phones and in English or Spanish. We also specifically included "How to read this" notes. All sources, assumptions, and limits are named.

We built this web app in TypeScript with React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, and Zod; ran the optimizer in a Web Worker; and deployed using Vercel. The data pipeline and exact linear-program checker were in Python using SciPy, pandas, and NumPy.
